chapter_title: A Friend Found in Music (Twin Melodies)
subject: English
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 50 minutes × 4 periods = 200 minutes
Total: 4 periods · 3h 20min

periods.activity_title: Reading the Poem and Appreciating Its Craft

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Reflect and Respond (p.194): oral sharing — favourite music, musicians, reasons
Reading for Appreciation (p.195): metaphors-to-similes, rhyme scheme, anaphora, mood, poet's purpose

time_bands.activity: Students share responses to Reflect and Respond (p.194): preferred music type, favourite musicians, and reasons for their choices. The teacher invites two or three students to speak briefly before opening a quick paired exchange, ensuring a variety of musical preferences surfaces.

The teacher reads the poem aloud with students following in their textbooks (p.194–195), then assigns students to re-read silently. The teacher draws attention to the anaphoric pattern of 'Music is…' and the ABCB rhyme scheme, prompting students to notice how the verse itself feels musical.

Students work through Reading for Appreciation (p.195): they identify the metaphors and rewrite them as similes, name the rhyme scheme and discuss its impact, explain the poet's purpose in repeating 'music', state the mood from the given options, and find evidence that the speaker is the poet herself. The teacher facilitates whole-class discussion, building toward the question of the poem's central message.

periods.teacher_notes: The poem's dominant device is metaphor — music compared to ocean, rhythm, therapy, and a needed friend — and students may conflate metaphor with simile initially; the metaphor-to-simile conversion task is an ideal corrective. The anaphoric repetition of 'Music is…' creates the meditative, incantatory quality the poem's appreciation summary describes; prompt students to read two stanzas aloud to feel this rhythm before they label it.
materials: Blackboard or chart for listing metaphors

periods.activity_title: Extract Analysis, Deep Comprehension, and Listening to a Musical Dilemma

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Critical Reflection (p.196): extract on therapy/blue — meaning, mood, central idea, true/false
Listen and Respond (p.199): predict answers before listening, then verify after

homework.task_brief: Check Your Understanding (p.196): five extended-answer questions on the poem's imagery, message, and appeal

time_bands.activity: Students locate the extract 'Music is the therapy / I need when I feel blue…' on p.196. The teacher leads a close reading of the extract: students interpret 'feel blue', identify the line showing music brings happiness, explain what 'pull through' signifies, judge the true/false statement, and select the central idea of the extract. Responses are shared and discussed as a class.

Students read the six Listen and Respond questions (p.199) silently and record their predictions about the speakers' relationship, location, instrument, problem, failed solution, and final decision. The teacher invites one or two predictions per question to activate prior knowledge before the audio.

The teacher reads the transcript aloud (or plays the recording) while students listen and check their predictions. After listening, students discuss any answers they needed to revise and explain what in the conversation gave them the correct information, consolidating comprehension of the santoor-practice dilemma.

periods.teacher_notes: The extract centres on music as emotional sustenance — the poem appreciation notes that this is the poem's dominant theme; encourage students to connect the phrase 'feel blue' to the broader metaphor of music-as-therapy rather than treating it as isolated idiom. For the listening segment, Jaspreet's problem (teacher visits only twice a week) is distinct from the failed solution (watching videos); students commonly conflate the two, so prompt them to re-state each in their own words.
materials: Transcript text (Unit 6, p.270 of transcript booklet)

periods.activity_title: Role Play on Music and Studies, then Phrasal Verbs in Context

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Speaking Activity (p.199): group role play — music teacher, two students, parent debating music and studies
Vocabulary in Context (p.197): classify emotion words; fill blanks with nostalgia/elation/anguish/melancholy/jubilant
Vocabulary in Context (p.198): match six 'move' phrasal verbs to their correct meanings

time_bands.activity: Groups of four assign roles — music teacher, Student 1 (doubtful), Student 2 (convinced), and parent — and prepare their role play using the cues on p.199. Two groups present to the class; the teacher guides them to use complete sentences, logical continuity, and to frame questions that sustain the conversation. Peer feedback focuses on argument quality and naturalness of exchange.

The class reads the emotion phrases from the poem — 'feel blue', 'lifts my spirits', 'most cheerful' — and classifies them as positive or negative emotions (p.197). Students then fill in the blanks choosing from nostalgia, elation, anguish, despondence, melancholy, and jubilant, with the teacher discussing why each contextual cue makes one option more precise than the other.

The teacher introduces phrasal verbs through the poem's 'pull through' and 'moves me', then students match the six 'move' phrasal verbs in the sentences on p.198 — move out, move in, move on, move over, move along, move off — to their meanings. The class checks answers together and the teacher highlights how the preposition or adverb shifts meaning entirely.

periods.teacher_notes: In the role play, students playing the doubtful student (Student 1) often struggle to generate counter-arguments; prompt them to draw on the poem's own ideas — music taking time away from study — to keep the exchange substantive. For the vocabulary task, 'despondence' and 'anguish' are the most commonly confused pair; the sentence context (a singer expressing intensity of emotion) points toward anguish, which is sharper and more physical than despondence.
materials: Blackboard for listing phrasal verb meanings

periods.activity_title: Drafting an Invitation Letter and Exploring Music as Therapy

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Writing Task (p.200): draft invitation letter to grandparents for World Music Day sitar recital
Learning Beyond the Text (p.201): research music as alternative therapy — Raga Chikitsa and Sangita Sudha

homework.task_brief: Learning Beyond the Text (p.201): collect poems and songs about music in English and your own language

time_bands.activity: The teacher introduces the writing task: a personal invitation letter to grandparents for a World Music Day sitar recital (p.200). The class reviews the required format together — sender's address, date, salutation, warm body, complimentary close — and the teacher highlights the difference between first-person warmth ('I') and the inclusive 'We' and 'You' expected in the body.

Students draft their invitation letters independently, following the format and language guidelines on p.200. The teacher circulates, offering formative feedback on tone, structure, and the inclusion of event details (21 June, venue, time). Students swap letters with a neighbour for a quick peer read, then revise a sentence or two based on feedback before finalising.

The teacher introduces the cultural heritage context: ancient Indian texts — Raga Chikitsa and Sangita Sudha — documented music's healing properties and emotional effects centuries ago. Students discuss in pairs what they know about music as therapy today, share examples, and the teacher draws out connections to the poem's portrayal of music as emotional sustenance, broadening the theme beyond the personal.

periods.teacher_notes: Students commonly write invitations in an impersonal or overly formal register; remind them that the addressees are grandparents and the style should be warm and affectionate, not bureaucratic. The cultural heritage discussion on Raga Chikitsa connects naturally to the poem's metaphor of music-as-therapy — this is an opportunity to link the poem's personal, intimate voice to a tradition that runs through centuries of Indian musical thought.

items.source_lo: Student analyses a poem's figurative language, tone, and structural devices using poetry as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Bryanna T. Perkins's poem using music metaphors — ocean, rhythm, therapy, needed friend — and anaphoric repetition.
items.item_stem: Which of the following best describes the tone of 'A Friend Found in Music' by Bryanna T. Perkins?

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student notices music is linked to sadness but misses the poem's overriding affirmation and uplift.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student focuses on the gentle rhyme without registering the intimate emotional sincerity of the speaker.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student may be misreading the anaphoric structure as clinical enumeration rather than personal declaration.

items.source_lo: Student analyses a poem's figurative language, tone, and structural devices using poetry as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Bryanna T. Perkins's poem using music metaphors — ocean, rhythm, therapy, needed friend — and anaphoric repetition.
items.item_stem:
1. In the third stanza, music is called 'the therapy / I need when I feel blue.' Identify the metaphor at work here and explain what it reveals about the speaker's relationship with music.
2. The poem opens with the metaphor 'Music is the ocean / That pulls me to the shore.' Analyse how the choice of the word 'pulls' contributes to the effect of this image — what does it suggest about the speaker's experience of music that a neutral word like 'brings' would not?
3. Discuss how the anaphoric repetition of 'Music is…' across all three stanzas shapes both the structure and the emotional impact of the poem.
items.visual_stimulus: Read the second stanza on p.195, beginning "Music is the therapy".

expected_elements: Metaphor: music as therapy — implies music heals emotional pain, not just entertains.
'Pulls' conveys irresistible, involuntary attraction; 'brings' is neutral and intentional.
Anaphora creates incantatory rhythm, making the poem itself feel like music.
Repetition builds cumulative emotional intensity across stanzas.
Each metaphor adds a new dimension: sustenance, healing, companionship.

items.source_lo: Student demonstrates active listening by predicting, verifying, and reflecting on information in a spoken conversation.
items.source_context: Jaspreet's santoor-practice dilemma at a music centre — problem, failed video solution, mother's resolution.
items.item_stem:
Listen to the conversation between Jaspreet and his mother. Decide whether each of the following statements is true or false, and write one sentence justifying your answer.
(1) Jaspreet wants to change to a different musical instrument.
(2) Jaspreet tried watching videos to improve his santoor playing, but found it unhelpful.
(3) Jaspreet's mother plans to buy a santoor immediately so he can practise at home.
(4) The teacher visits the music centre only twice a week.

options.text: Jaspreet tried watching videos to improve his santoor playing, but found it unhelpful.
Jaspreet wants to change to a different musical instrument.
Jaspreet's mother plans to buy a santoor immediately so he can practise at home.
The teacher visits the music centre only twice a week.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: (1) False — Jaspreet fears he may have to change instruments, but his mother reassures him this will not be necessary. (2) True — Jaspreet explicitly says watching videos did not help because playing is a hands-on skill. (3) False — his mother arranges to borrow a santoor from a friend until they can purchase their own. (4) True — Jaspreet says the teacher comes to the centre only twice a week, making regular practice difficult.

items.source_lo: Student demonstrates active listening by predicting, verifying, and reflecting on information in a spoken conversation.
items.source_context: Jaspreet's santoor-practice dilemma at a music centre — problem, failed video solution, mother's resolution.
items.item_stem: Jaspreet's mother suggests borrowing a santoor from a friend rather than immediately purchasing one. What does this solution reveal about how she balances Jaspreet's enthusiasm for music with practical concerns? Use evidence from the conversation to support your answer.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: The mother's solution — borrowing a santoor from a friend — shows she takes Jaspreet's passion seriously while being cautious about immediate expenditure; she addresses the root cause (inability to practise at home) without a premature financial commitment, demonstrating both supportiveness and pragmatism.

items.source_context: Group role play debating whether music classes benefit or burden a student's academic life.
items.item_stem: Describe a situation in which a student might feel that taking up an instrument is conflicting with their studies. What would you say to reassure that student, drawing on ideas about music's value from your reading and your own experience?

expected_elements: Clearly describes a plausible conflict scenario (exams, homework pressure).
Draws on at least one idea about music's emotional or cognitive benefit.
Addresses the student's concern directly with a specific reassurance.
Uses complete sentences and a conversational but persuasive tone.
Shows awareness of the other person's perspective before offering a counter-view.

items.item_stem: Your school is debating the motion: 'Music education should be a compulsory part of every school's timetable.' Argue either for or against this motion, supporting your position with at least two distinct reasons and responding to one likely objection from the opposing side.

expected_elements: States a clear position on the motion at the outset.
Provides two distinct, developed reasons supporting the position.
Anticipates and addresses one counter-argument from the opposing side.
Uses formal debating register — structured, reasoned, not merely emotive.
Concludes with a confident restatement or call-to-action.

items.source_context: A student performing at a community concert writes to invite elderly relatives to the event.
items.item_stem: Your neighbourhood cultural society is hosting an evening of Indian classical music to mark the anniversary of a local music school. You have been asked to perform on stage. Write an informal letter to your aunt and uncle, who live in another city, inviting them to attend. Your letter should: mention the occasion and what makes it special; include relevant details such as date, time, and venue; write in a warm and personal style using first and second person; follow the correct format for a personal letter.

expected_elements: Correct personal letter format: address, date, salutation, body, close.
Warm, first-person register — not formal or impersonal in tone.
Event details (occasion, date, time, venue) clearly stated in the body.
Personal connection made — asks about the relatives' well-being before the request.
Complimentary close appropriate to the relationship (e.g. Yours affectionately).

items.item_stem: A local newspaper has published an editorial arguing that arts and music programmes in schools should be reduced to allow more time for science and mathematics. Write a letter to the editor expressing your disagreement with this view. Your letter should: state your position clearly in the opening; provide two or three reasoned arguments in support of arts education; address one point from the editorial's argument; use a formal and persuasive register appropriate to a letter to the editor.

expected_elements: Formal letter-to-editor format and register maintained throughout.
Clear position stated in the opening paragraph without ambiguity.
Two or three distinct, developed arguments for arts education.
Engages with and rebuts the editorial's core claim about time allocation.
Concluding appeal to the editor or readership with a call to reconsider.

items.source_context: Emotion words from the poem and 'move'-based phrasal verbs used in music-related sentences.
items.item_stem: Match each emotion word in Column A with its correct meaning in Column B.
items.visual_stimulus:
| Column A | Column B |
|---|---|
| elation | a deep, quiet sadness or sorrow |
| melancholy | a longing or wistful affection for the past |
| nostalgia | a joyful excitement and high spirits |
| anguish | severe emotional distress or suffering |
| despondence | a loss of hope and low spirits |

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: elation – c, melancholy – a, nostalgia – b, anguish – d, despondence – e

answer_key.right: a joyful excitement and high spirits
a deep, quiet sadness or sorrow
a longing or wistful affection for the past
a loss of hope and low spirits

items.source_lo: Student identifies and applies emotion-related vocabulary and phrasal verbs in context using poetry's language as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Emotion words from the poem and 'move'-based phrasal verbs used in music-related sentences.
items.item_stem:
The poem uses the phrasal verb 'pull through' to describe how music helps the speaker overcome difficulty. For each of the following sentences, replace the underlined phrasal verb with a single word or phrase of equivalent meaning, then write a new sentence of your own using the same phrasal verb in a different context related to music or learning.

(1) After months of struggling with the tabla, Ramesh finally moved on to more complex rhythms.
(2) The orchestra moved off the stage in silence after the final note faded.
(3) The young violinist asked her stand partner to move over so she could see the conductor better.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: (1) 'moved on' = progressed / advanced; e.g. 'After practising scales for weeks, she moved on to her first sonata.' (2) 'moved off' = departed / left; e.g. 'The band moved off the stage after their encore.' (3) 'moved over' = shifted / made room; e.g. 'He moved over on the bench so the new student could sit beside him at the keyboard.'

items.source_lo: Student explores the cultural and historical dimensions of a theme through research and interdisciplinary connections.
items.source_context: India's tradition of music as healing — Raga Chikitsa, Sangita Sudha, and contemporary music therapy.
items.item_stem: The poem describes music as 'the therapy I need when I feel blue.' India has a long tradition of understanding music's healing power — texts such as Raga Chikitsa and the seventeenth-century Sangita Sudha document the effects of specific ragas on emotions and well-being. In a paragraph of eight to ten sentences, explain what these ancient texts tell us about the relationship between music and human emotions, and connect their insights to the poem's central claim that music is an emotional companion.

expected_elements: Names Raga Chikitsa and Sangita Sudha and states their historical context.
Explains that specific ragas were documented to affect particular emotions.
Connects the ancient therapeutic view of music to the poem's metaphor of music-as-therapy.
Shows understanding that this tradition gives the poem's personal voice a wider cultural grounding.
Response is coherent, eight to ten sentences, in the student's own words.

items.source_lo: Student explores the cultural and historical dimensions of a theme through research and interdisciplinary connections.
items.source_context: India's tradition of music as healing — Raga Chikitsa, Sangita Sudha, and contemporary music therapy.
items.item_stem: Design a research project titled 'Music Across Cultures as Healer.' Your project should: identify two or three traditions from different parts of the world (including at least one Indian tradition) that use music for emotional or physical healing; describe the methods or forms of music used in each tradition; compare how these traditions understand the relationship between music and well-being; and explain how your findings deepen your understanding of why Bryanna T. Perkins calls music 'the therapy I need.' Present your plan as a structured outline with section headings.

expected_elements: Identifies at least two cultures' healing music traditions, one Indian.
Describes specific methods or musical forms used in each tradition.
Offers a meaningful comparison — similarity or contrast — across traditions.
Connects research findings explicitly to the poem's 'therapy' metaphor.
Presents work as a structured outline with clear section headings.
